note:
Vol. II No. 6, the second issue after the resumption, and the one that starts the two series this epic will lean on hardest: the CHICAGO PRICES CURRENT, corrected weekly, and the ARRIVALS OF VESSELS AT CHICAGO. Both run in every issue from here to the scene date. The prices current carries a BUILDING MATERIALS block — lumber, shingles, square timber, brick, stone, lime, wood — which is the first thing in this corpus that prices what the town was made of.

The reading is uneven because the transcription is. Pages 1, 2 and 4 are national reprint matter and their columns are damaged by systematic line-start clipping; page 3 columns 3-6 are the town and are legible. Fourteen claims, all but two off page 3.

claims.notes:
WHAT CHICAGO WAS BUILT OF, AND WHAT IT COST, FIVE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. The seven-line Building Materials block is the most directly usable price series this corpus has produced: assorted lumber at $28-29 the thousand feet, shingles at $3.00-3.50 the thousand, square timber at 5-6 cents the running foot, BRICK AT $5-6 THE THOUSAND, stone at $6.00-6.50 the cord, lime at 75-88 cents the barrel, firewood at $2.50 the cord.

BRICK AT $5-6 A THOUSAND IS THE NUMBER TO KEEP. It says brick was a quoted, weekly-traded commodity in Chicago in May 1835 and not an exotic import — which is the background against which 'Hubbard & Co's. brick store' (1835-06-11) reads as a deliberate choice rather than a curiosity, and against which the reconstruction's overwhelmingly timber town is the right default with brick as the marked exception.

THE FIGURES ARE READ OFF A DAMAGED TABLE AND SOME CELLS ARE EMPTY. The transcription sets the table as running text with the column rules gone, so the reading depends on the units printed beside each row ('bbl', 'bush', 'lb', 'cord', '1000 ft') and on the two-figure a-b range form. Where a figure did not survive, the normalized reading leaves a bracketed gap rather than supplying it — fine flour, wheat's low, and wood's high are all incomplete here and can be read whole off 1835-06-04 and 1835-06-10, which print the same table.

THE SERIES MOVES, AND FAST. Superfine flour is $5.00-6.50 here; $10.00-12.00 on 1835-06-04, when the editor writes that 'our stock of eatables is almost exhausted'; and $15.00-16.00 on 1835-06-24. THE BUILDING MATERIALS DO NOT MOVE AT ALL across those five weeks — every figure in the block is identical in all three printings. Food tripled while brick, lumber and lime held. That contrast is a finding about the town's summer of 1835 and it is why all three tables are quoted rather than only one.

TWELVE ARRIVALS IN A WEEK, and the first list in this corpus with dates against the entries. Two brigs (Woolsey and Indiana, both from Buffalo) and ten schooners and a sloop working Buffalo, Cleveland, Green Bay and St. Joseph. The 20th and the 22nd carry six between them, which is a week's worth of unloading for a harbor with no wharf frontage to speak of.

THE DATE COLUMN IS PARTLY LOST and the entries above 'May 20' cannot be dated, so no individual date is asserted beyond the four the transcription actually prints (20, 23, 24, 2[5], 2[6]). The Llewellyn appears here for the first time and is advertised in the same issue as the new Chicago and St. Joseph packet, which is how a hull in a marine list becomes a scheduled service.

claims.notes:
THE POSTMASTER MARRIES, and the notice is worth its space for the four words after his name: 'Postmaster, Chicago Ill.' John S. C. Hogan signed the 1 January 1834 letter list (read by T-0310), keeps the store 'one door below the Post Office' in South Water Street, and is still postmaster on 27 April 1835. That closes a sixteen-month chain on one man holding one office, which is what lets his store anchor the Post Office's position at the scene date.

THE PLACE OF THE MARRIAGE IS NOT CHICAGO — near Lewiston, Fulton County — and the bride and her grandfather are 'of the former place'. So Anne Maria Barney and Capt. Leonard are minted as PEOPLE and are NOT given Chicago as a place; she presumably comes to the town after 27 April, and this notice does not say she had by 1 July.

THE FORT IS GARRISONED AT THE SCENE DATE AND HERE IS ITS COMMANDING OFFICER, BY NAME AND REGIMENT: Major J. Green, 5th Infantry, commanding the post. That is a fact the reconstruction of Fort Dearborn wants on its own, and it is corroborated three weeks later by Lt. L. T. Jamison advertising over the same fort for beef, wood and hay contracts (1835-06-04). The initial is read 'J.' — 'S. GREEN' in the 1835-06-10 printing and '. GREEN' here, so it is left as printed in `as_printed` and the reading is stated as uncertain between J and S nowhere else than in this note, because the surname and the office are not in doubt and the initial is.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT THE TOWN. United States arms and accoutrements were 'in the hands of citizens of the country' in numbers worth a standing advertisement and a threat of prosecution — the residue of the militia and the 1832 war, being called back in three years later. It is the only military notice in this reading range that addresses civilians rather than contractors.

claims.notes:
A FIRM FORMING, NOT DISSOLVING — the other side of ruling 3, and dated 26 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. Three named partners, one of whom (Byram King) is also Clerk of School District No. 4 in June and is on the town-meeting committee of seven. The house is already trading under the name in the 1835-05-18 white fish notice, so 'have formed a connection' formalises something running.

THE PLACEMENT IS `none` AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. Jones, King & Co. never advertise their own address in any of these eight issues; the street is known only because OTHER people place themselves against them — J. Curtiss is 'first [door] west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co.' in South Water Street, and the Democrat is printed 'over Messrs Jones & King['s] Hard[ware]'. The `street` field carries South Water Street on that chain; the `placement` does not, because this advertisement offers no offset of its own to place anything against. An anchor with no self-stated position is exactly the shape T-0263 will have to resolve.

BY 1835-06-17 the firm is advertising for 'one copper smith, and one tin and sheet iron worker' and acting as agents for Avery's Patent rotary engines — so within a month of forming they are hiring metal tradesmen, which suggests a workshop behind the store and not only a counter.

claims.notes:
THIS IS THE CLAIM THAT PLACES THE EXCHANGE COFFEE HOUSE — CORNER OF LAKE AND FRANKLIN STREETS — and the Exchange is where the town held its Democratic meeting of 13 April 1835 and its town-election caucus of 6 June 1835. A named public house on a named corner, stated incidentally by a lawyer giving his own address, is worth more than either meeting notice, because neither of them says where the house was.

AND IT PLACES HEACOCK: second storey, OPPOSITE that corner. 'Opposite' across which of the two streets is not stated, so this fixes him to one of the three other corners of the intersection and no further. Recorded as `corner` on the anchor rather than as `relative`, because the evidence is an intersection and not a door-count.

EIGHT YEARS A RESIDENT, said in 1835, puts Heacock in Chicago from 1827 — before the town was platted. He is one of the very few people in this corpus who states his own arrival, and he states it to sell land-agency work, which is a reason to believe it (his customers could check) and a reason to record it as his claim rather than as fact.

THE TEXT CHANGES BETWEEN PRINTINGS in a way worth keeping: this one says he is 'having the commission [of] the peace'; from 1835-06-04 it says 'being a Justice of the peace'. Same man, firmer claim, one week later.

Set that beside the same month's 'every room of our public houses' being full and the picture is a town short of lodging and not short of shops.

TEMPLE is the same man who wants 'fifteen strong work Horses' in the 1835-06-04 issue and who sits on the town meeting's committee of seven on 16 June — a substantial figure, and this notice attaches property on two streets to him. THREE PARTS OF THE TOWN NAMED IN ONE LINE — the School Section, the river frontage, and the original town — which is a private seller's own geography of Chicago six weeks before the scene date, and it matches the plat the reconstruction stands on. 'the original town' is the 1830 canal-commissioners' plat; the School Section is section 16, subdivided and sold in 1833; 'on the river' is frontage. Nothing here places a single lot, and nothing should be inferred about which; the value is the vocabulary.

E. K. Hubbard chairs the town meeting of 16 June 1835 and is the agent for the Rezigue dwelling in Kinzie's Addition, so he is a principal in the town's property trade in exactly these weeks. He is a different man from the 'Hubbard & Co.' of the brick store in La Salle Street and from 'Col. G. S. Hubbard' who calls the town meeting to order; this pass does NOT merge the three, and T-0299's identity work is where that belongs.

That is worth saying plainly rather than dropping the claim: the moment any witness locates the clerk's office, Casey goes on the ground with it, and the May 1835 term of that court sat in this town (same issue, page 2 column 5), so the office was a real address in the town and not a county seat elsewhere.

The 1835-06-10 issue closes the story — the term ended on the Monday with nearly two hundred causes docketed and two criminal indictments, and Judge Breese gave universal satisfaction in his first term here. Between them the two paragraphs say the town supported a court with a two-hundred-cause docket five weeks before the scene date.

THE COLUMN IS SHREDDED and this paragraph runs beside an unrelated one line for line, so the left edge of every line is lost.
